name: Potassium
lead: Potassium is an essential mineral and the main positively charged ion (cation) inside cells. It supports nerve signalling, muscle and heart contraction, and the maintenance of fluid balance and normal kidney function.[1][12][14] It is obtained from foods such as potatoes, beans, fruit and dairy, and is also sold as supplements and as potassium chloride medicines.

In looksmaxxing and depuffing discussions, potassium is mentioned because the balance between sodium and potassium influences how the body handles fluid. Higher potassium intake promotes sodium excretion and has been found to lower blood pressure in trials.[3] No published trial in the sources reviewed has tested potassium intake or supplements for facial puffiness.
Excess potassium (hyperkalaemia) is dangerous, and reviews and trials describe it in the context of kidney disease and drugs that raise potassium.[8][11]

paras: Potassium is discussed in depuffing contexts as part of electrolyte and sodium management. The idea is that a diet higher in potassium and lower in sodium supports normal fluid regulation, and that this might reduce visible puffiness. The sources reviewed contain no test of this idea for the face.

Potassium chloride is prescribed for the treatment and prevention of hypokalaemia in people for whom dietary measures or diuretic dose reduction are not sufficient.[14] Randomised trials have tested raising plasma potassium to high-normal levels in people at risk of ventricular arrhythmias and in preventing atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery.[7][10] A meta-analysis of trials lasting four weeks or more examined the dose-response relation between potassium intake and blood pressure.[3]

Common adverse effects of oral potassium salts include nausea, vomiting, flatulence, abdominal pain and diarrhoea. Solid forms can produce ulcerative or narrowing lesions of the gastrointestinal tract if they remain in contact with the mucosa.[14]

Hyperkalaemia is life-threatening and a potential cause of cardiac arrest; its acute treatment has been reviewed in a 2025 meta-analysis.[11] Drugs that raise potassium, such as the mineralocorticoid antagonist finerenone, carry a measured risk of hyperkalaemia in people with chronic kidney disease.[8] Grokipedia notes that higher intakes from food are generally safe in healthy individuals with normal kidney function because excess is excreted by the kidneys, whereas supplements pose greater risks.[2] For pregnancy, the US label states that supplementation not leading to hyperkalaemia is not expected to cause fetal harm, but no human data exist for the extended-release tablets.[14]

Potassium is the principal intracellular cation, at roughly 150 to 160 mEq per litre inside cells compared with 3.5 to 5 mEq per litre in plasma, and it participates in intracellular tonicity, nerve impulse transmission, muscle contraction and normal renal function.[14] Its homeostasis is tightly regulated by the kidneys and hormones.[13]
Potassium metal was first isolated in 1807 by Humphry Davy by electrolysis of molten caustic potash, the first metal isolated this way; the name derives from 'potash', plant ashes boiled in pots.[1]
No studies found on potassium for facial puffiness or cosmetic depuffing.

Related clinical research in other settings: a 2020 dose-response meta-analysis of randomised trials examined potassium supplementation and blood pressure;[3] a 2025 Danish multicentre trial in the New England Journal of Medicine tested raising potassium in people with implantable defibrillators;[7] the TIGHT K trial examined potassium supplementation to prevent atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery;[10] and a Frontiers trial examined magnesium and potassium for insomnia in diabetes.[9] Registered trials include dietary potassium liberalisation in pre-dialysis patients and a potassium intake-response trial in hypertension.[15][16]
